solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Basic floor design requires a ruler

parts.note: a design or scheme is a plan
a king is a ruler

explanation.surface: Laying out a simple floor calls for a measuring ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruler' suggests the measuring stick a floor-layer needs, but here it is a monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Planks laid side by side make the most elementary kind of wooden flooring.

clue.text: Brigand swaps sides to be Roman governor

indicators.note: sides are right and left, so the R for right is swapped for L for left

parts.note: a pirate is a brigand of the sea

explanation.surface: An outlaw changes allegiance and becomes a Roman official.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swaps sides' means R (right) becomes L (left).
explanation.definitionFit: Pontius Pilate was the Roman prefect of Judaea at the trial of Jesus.

clue.text: A nurse takes time to be there

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: takes says the nurse takes in the time beside it

parts.note: to nurse is to tend

explanation.surface: A nurse spends time being present for a patient.
explanation.definitionFit: To attend a meeting or event is to be present at it.

clue.text: A country's livelihood, you could say

indicators.note: you could say signals that the word for livelihood is spoken, not spelt

parts.note: a career is one's livelihood

explanation.surface: A nation's means of making a living.
explanation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic British accent the word for a livelihood sounds just like the country.
explanation.definitionFit: Korea is a nation of East Asia, now split into North and South.

clue.text: Frontline caught in seething rain — such bliss!

indicators.note: caught in says the frontline is held inside the other letters
seething means churning, so the letters of rain are stirred up

parts.note: the van, short for vanguard, is the front line of an army

explanation.surface: A front line soldier caught in a raging downpour, sarcastically called bliss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seething' scrambles the rain and 'caught in' holds the frontline inside; the exclamation 'such bliss!' is ironic in the surface, but straight as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: In Buddhism nirvana is the state of perfect bliss and release from suffering.

clue.text: Socialist author unhappy with Blair?

parts.note: reads as a left-wing writer disliking Tony Blair, but this writer's real surname was Blair: Eric Blair took a pen name

explanation.surface: A left-wing writer disapproves of New Labour's prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: The author of Animal Farm was born Eric Blair and wrote under a pen name, perhaps unhappy with his own name; as a socialist he would also dislike Tony Blair's politics.
explanation.definitionFit: The socialist writer of Nineteen Eighty-Four was born Eric Arthur Blair.

clue.text: Strange insects biting in cattle

indicators.note: biting says the strange insects close their jaws on the word in

parts.note: rum is old slang for strange
ants are insects
taken as written

explanation.surface: Odd insects are biting the cows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'biting' has the two outer pieces closing on the middle word, which ends up sitting between them rather than inside either.
explanation.definitionFit: Cattle chew the cud, making them examples of cud-chewing mammals.

clue.text: Start off being miserable and you'll get the sack

indicators.note: start off says the first letter is removed

parts.note: dejection is the state of being miserable

explanation.surface: Gloom at work will get you fired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Start off' drops the D of DEJECTION.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting the sack is being thrown out of a job, an expulsion.

clue.text: Flyers from sale left scattered around

indicators.note: scattered around says the letters are strewn into a new order

explanation.surface: Advertising handouts from a sale lie strewn about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scattered around' rearranges SALE LEFT.
explanation.definitionFit: Flyers are printed handbills, the same as handouts distributed in the street.

clue.text: Like Shakespeare's genius it rarely goes amiss

indicators.note: going amiss means going wrong, so these letters are put out of order

explanation.surface: A claim that the Bard's talent seldom fails.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes amiss' rearranges IT RARELY.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's gift was a gift for writing, so it is of the written, bookish kind.

clue.text: One cell with a ring fixed in a beam, perhaps

indicators.note: fixed in says the ring is set inside the other letters
perhaps signals that the words a beam stand for another arrangement of their letters

parts.note: a ring is round like the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone fits a ring into a wooden beam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges A BEAM to AMEBA, itself the American spelling; 'fixed in' then puts the O inside it after the M.
explanation.definitionFit: The amoeba is the classic single-celled organism of biology lessons.

clue.text: Obscure leaders in battle located under ruins

indicators.note: leaders in means the first letter of each following word

explanation.surface: Commanders are found in a bunker beneath the rubble of battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaders in' takes the first letters of battle, located, under, ruins.
explanation.definitionFit: To blur something is to make it indistinct, to obscure it.

clue.text: Valiant nil-nil replay is futile …

indicators.note: a replay is a match played again, here letters played again in a new order

parts.note: a nil-nil score is two zeros, each read as the letter O

explanation.surface: A brave goalless draw is not worth a replay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'replay' rearranges VALIANT with the two Os of nil-nil.
explanation.definitionFit: An effort that is to no avail achieves nothing, which is exactly what futile means.

clue.text: … in return, City beat Brazilian port

indicators.note: in return means the whole run of letters is read backwards

parts.note: LA, Los Angeles, is the classic crossword city
to tan someone's hide is to beat them

explanation.surface: Continuing the football story: a city side wins the return leg.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links it to the previous clue's football surface; 'in return' reverses LATAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Natal is a port city in north-east Brazil, capital of Rio Grande do Norte.

clue.text: Sensible patients wouldn't be in it

definitions.text: Sensible patients wouldn't be in it

parts.words: Sensible patients wouldn't be in it
parts.note: sensible reads as level-headed, but here means conscious, able to sense

explanation.surface: Patients with good sense would avoid a certain place or situation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sensible' in its old sense means aware or conscious; an unconscious patient is in a deep state.
explanation.definitionFit: A deep state of unconsciousness is one no conscious patient can be in.

clue.text: Tubs are OK to contain explosions

indicators.note: containing explosions means bottling up a blast, so the words tubs are ok are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Tubs are judged suitable for holding explosions.
explanation.walkthrough: The indicator is loose: the explosions themselves, as contained, rearrange TUBS ARE OK.
explanation.definitionFit: Outbreaks of violence or disease are sudden eruptions, like blasts.

clue.text: River in swollen condition — sound the alarm!

parts.note: taken as written
gout is a disease that swells the joints

explanation.surface: A river in flood, so raise the alarm!
explanation.walkthrough: 'swollen condition' suggests a river in spate; it is the joint ailment.
explanation.definitionFit: Bells or alarms ring out when they sound loudly to warn people.

clue.text: Pathetic feeling

definitions.meaning: feeling by contact with the hand

explanation.definitionFit: A touching story is moving, and touching is also physically feeling something.

clue.text: Any issue he raised couldn't succeed

definitions.text: Any issue he raised couldn't succeed

parts.words: Any issue he raised couldn't succeed
parts.note: reads as a politician whose causes fail, but issue means children who cannot inherit the title

explanation.surface: A man whose every proposal fails.
explanation.walkthrough: In the British House of Lords, a peerage granted for life only cannot pass to the holder's children.
explanation.definitionFit: A life peerage dies with its holder, so no heir succeeds to it.

clue.text: Deleted word for "glove" in dictionary

indicators.note: in says one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: OED is the Oxford English Dictionary
a mitt is a kind of glove

explanation.surface: A lexicographer has removed a synonym for glove from the dictionary.
explanation.definitionFit: Something left out or struck from a text has been cut, like a removed word.

clue.text: Frank's caught out with ominous results

indicators.note: out says the letters for caught are taken from the word for frank

parts.note: direct means frank, with 's for has

explanation.surface: Frank is found out, with dreadful consequences.
explanation.definitionFit: Dire consequences are dreadful, foretelling disaster.

clue.text: Airline's eastern centre of operations

parts.note: BA, British Airways, with its possessive s

explanation.surface: An airline's hub in the east.
explanation.definitionFit: A base is the headquarters from which an organisation runs its activity.

clue.text: Support needed on journal, work piling up

parts.note: to back is to support
a log is a journal or record

explanation.surface: Backing for a diary as work accumulates.
explanation.definitionFit: A backlog is an accumulation of unfinished tasks.

clue.text: Hard workers, we're told, who can't vote?

indicators.note: we're told signals that the word for hard workers is heard, not spelt

parts.note: miners do hard work underground

explanation.surface: Diligent workers who have no vote.
explanation.walkthrough: Under-18s cannot vote in British elections.
explanation.definitionFit: Young people below the age of majority are not entitled to vote.

clue.text: Soar aloft, like Chelsea's first goal

parts.note: as means like

indicators.note: first means the opening letter of the next word

parts.note: an end is an aim or goal

explanation.surface: A Chelsea striker's opening goal soars into the net.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goal' suggests football but means an aim.
explanation.definitionFit: To ascend is to climb or rise up into the air.

clue.text: Set free of charges yet bound over

definitions.meaning: to jump over a fence or bar

explanation.definitionFit: A court may acquit a defendant of charges, and a jumper may leap over a hurdle.

clue.text: Garden features using stones around lake

indicators.note: around says the stones go on either side of the lake

parts.note: rocks are stones
Erie is one of North America's Great Lakes

explanation.surface: A garden designer builds features with stones placed round a pond.
explanation.definitionFit: Rock gardens planted among stones are a familiar feature of British gardens.

clue.text: Prod to which toast's often attached

explanation.definitionFit: To urge someone is to spur them, and eggs are often served on toast.

clue.text: One cold March back in the Antarctic eg

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

indicators.note: back means the word for march is read backwards

parts.note: to march is to pace

explanation.surface: A single chilly March returns in the far south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'March' looks like the month but is the verb, and 'back' turns it round; 'the Antarctic eg' defines by example.
explanation.definitionFit: The Antarctic is covered by a permanent sheet of polar ice, an example of one.

clue.text: Upholder of standards

parts.note: reads as a guardian of moral standards, but standards here are flags

explanation.surface: Someone who defends principles.
explanation.definitionFit: A pole holds a standard, a military or royal banner, aloft.

clue.text: Tasteless ingredient of vinegar is harmful

indicators.note: ingredient of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A warning that vinegar can do you harm.
explanation.definitionFit: Something gaudy and vulgar in appearance shows no good taste.

clue.text: Wrongly diagnose, thus suffered a lot

indicators.note: wrongly says the letters of the next word are set out incorrectly

explanation.surface: A misdiagnosed patient went through great pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrongly' rearranges DIAGNOSE.
explanation.definitionFit: To have agonised is to have endured great anguish or worry.
